section_summary: The section concludes a July 1949 paper on Japanese city assemblies, covering their procedures, powers, relations with mayors, and duties to the public. It then begins Paper No. 4 of the Local Autonomy Program for the Cities of Japan, which explains municipal administration, civil service, and organizational design, with examples from three Japanese cities.

subfiles.title: The Local Autonomy Program for the Cities of Japan: City Assembly
subfiles.about: Guidance on the procedures, authority, conduct, and public responsibilities of Japanese city assemblies.
subfiles.summary: The paper explains assembly sessions, quorums, committees, voting, discipline, legislative and investigative powers, finance, and public access. It compares Japanese arrangements with those in England and the United States, urges orderly deliberation, and describes the assembly’s dealings with the mayor and city commissions. Its conclusion encourages assembly members to enact useful by-laws and plan city government carefully.

subfiles.title: The Local Autonomy Program for the Cities of Japan, Paper No. 4: Municipal Administration
subfiles.from: Headquarters Eighth United States Army, Civil Affairs Section, Legal and Government Division
subfiles.about: Explains how city administrations should carry out public policy and organize personnel and services.
subfiles.summary: The paper traces municipal policy from voters through elected officials to administrative execution, emphasizing orderly procedures and public service. It advocates a merit based civil service, adequate salaries, clear lines of authority, and functional divisions. It describes the mayor’s supervisory role and typical Japanese municipal sections, then gives organizational examples for Matsumoto, Miyakonojō, and Kashiwazaki. The paper continues beyond page 301.
